answer.label: Written by
answer.sourceLine: This is a genuine line from Marcus Aurelius’s Meditations, Book VII, section 27. The exact English wording is George Long’s 1862 translation; Marcus himself wrote it in Koine Greek as a private note to himself around 170–180 AD.

source.heading: The source
source.excerpt: Think not so much of what thou hast not as of what thou hast: but of the things which thou hast select the best, and then reflect how eagerly they would have been sought, if thou hadst them not. At the same time however take care that thou dost not through being so pleased with them accustom thyself to overvalue them, so as to be disturbed if ever thou shouldst not have them.
trail: The line appears verbatim in Book Seven of the George Long translation of the Meditations ↗, hosted by the Internet Classics Archive.
Wikiquote ↗ lists it in its sourced quotes under Book VII, 27 — not in any “Disputed” or “Misattributed” section.
The English is George Long’s, first published in 1862 ↗ as The Thoughts of the Emperor M. Aurelius Antoninus; the underlying Greek is Marcus’s own.
source.excerptNote: The full section (VII.27) in George Long’s 1862 translation. The widely-shared version usually stops at “if thou hadst them not,” dropping Marcus’s follow-up warning against becoming attached to those same possessions.

The specific English wording quoted here is George Long’s translation, first published in 1862 — well before 1931 — so this translation is also in the public domain in the United States.

author.name: Marcus Aurelius
author.heading: Marcus Aurelius
author.bio: Marcus Aurelius Antoninus (121–180 AD) was Roman emperor from 161 until his death and the last of the “Five Good Emperors.” His Meditations — a private notebook of Stoic reflections written in Greek during his military campaigns, never intended for publication — became one of the most enduring works of Stoic philosophy. This line is a characteristic Stoic exercise in gratitude and detachment.

misattribution.heading: A genuine quote — with a catch
misattribution.intro: This one is real: it is authentic Marcus Aurelius. The only things worth flagging are how the wording travels.

items.scope: The words are a translation, not Marcus’s literal phrasing
items.why: The archaic “thou hast / hadst” English is George Long’s 1862 rendering ↗. Marcus wrote in Greek; other translators (Hays, Farquharson, Hard) word VII.27 quite differently, so quoting these exact words as if Marcus “said” them is a translator’s voice, not the emperor’s.

The popular form stops at “if thou hadst them not,” turning it into a tidy gratitude aphorism. Marcus’s actual section VII.27 ↗ continues with a Stoic caution against over-valuing those same things — the balance that makes it Stoic rather than merely sentimental.

misattribution.truthLine: Authentic Marcus Aurelius, Meditations VII.27 ↗ — just remember the words are George Long’s 1862 translation, and the full passage carries a second, less-quoted half.

context.heading: Why it mattered
lead: The Meditations were never written for an audience. They are the private journal of a working emperor — jotted, in Greek, during campaigns on the Danube frontier — reminding himself how to live. Section VII.27 is one such reminder: a small mental exercise for redirecting attention from lack toward possession.

Its Stoic point is not simple positive thinking. Marcus tells himself to imagine his blessings as if he did not have them (a technique later called negative visualization) — and then, in the same breath, warns against clinging to them, so that losing them would not disturb his peace.
detailsBody: The commonly shared version omits Marcus’s closing caution: “take care that thou dost not… overvalue them, so as to be disturbed if ever thou shouldst not have them.” The full passage is about equanimity, not acquisition.
